questions.text: What exactly is in the emailed link and the queued job? Is the link the /reset?token=RAW page, and which base address does the server use to build it?
What is the "breached list" and where does it live (local file, table, external service)? How does the server look a password up in it?
questions.about: validate password: len >= 12 AND not in breached list

questions.text: What is the "email queue/worker" here: what stores the jobs, how does the worker pick them up, and what does "3 retries, then drop" mean in practice (timing, where a dropped job goes)?
What are `sessions`, and how does a login create a row there? What does the API do on each request when the session row is missing?

On step 3 of the submit flow, the 'password was changed' email is enqueued after COMMIT. If the server dies between COMMIT and the enqueue, or the enqueue fails, what does the user see and what happens?
When a user hits the 3-per-hour limit, what do they see? Is the generic message really the only feedback, and how would they know to wait?
Which email address does the reset link go to, and how is the user looked up (case, whitespace, multiple accounts with the same address)?
What does the 'generic error' page in a DB failure at submit look like, and does it keep the new password the user typed? Can they resubmit the same form?

answers.text: The link is <APP_BASE_URL>/reset?token=RAW, where APP_BASE_URL is a web-app config value; the job carries the recipient address and that link. Chosen so the click lands on the GET /reset page already in the design.
The brief only says 'the breached-password list' and does not say where it lives or how it is queried. The flow needs only accept/reject, so I added an open question and left the mechanism out.

Per the brief: the API adds a job to the existing email queue, a worker sends it through the third-party mail provider, retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. I do not know what stores the jobs, the exact backoff timing, or whether a dropped job goes anywhere besides the log. Not needed by this design; I added a line in the notes that says what the worker does.

Per the brief, sessions has one row per logged-in device and the API checks it on every request, so deleting the row logs that device out. I do not know the exact login insert or the response (likely 401) when the row is missing; this design does not depend on either. Noted in the Logout line.

Simplest handling: the reset already committed and stands. If the enqueue fails it is logged, the user is still redirected to /login, and no notice email is sent. If the server dies between COMMIT and enqueue, the user sees a browser error, but the password is changed and they can log in. No retry mechanism is added. Table row added.
They see only the fixed generic message, as the brief requires, so they are not told to wait; if no email arrives they will retry and get the same message. Added to the failure table.

The link goes to the email on the matched user row. I do not know whether users.email is unique or case-normalised. I decided to trim and lowercase the input and assume uniqueness; recorded as an open question.

A plain 'something went wrong, please try again' page. The transaction rolled back, so the link is still live. The server does not store the typed password; the user goes back and submits again with the same link. Added to the failure table.

questions.text: In step 2 of the submit flow, the password is validated first and the token is only checked in the UPDATE. If the link is already dead when the user submits a weak password, what do they see: the form with a reason, or the expired page?
How does the form on the GET /reset page send the token back? You say RAW is kept in the form; is it a hidden field, and does the POST URL carry it too?
questions.about: render "choose a new password" form (RAW kept in the form)

questions.text: Can the rate-limit count include rows that are already used or superseded? E.g. a user who requested 3 links, then successfully reset, is blocked from requesting for the rest of the hour?
questions.about: Rate limit = count(rows for user_id with issued_at > now()-1h)

questions.text: Between COMMIT of the new token and the enqueue, the old link is already dead and the new one has not been sent. If the enqueue fails, what does the user have, and how do they recover given the 3/hour limit?
What does the user see on POST /forgot-password when the email is unknown: is the response truly the same 200 body, and does the client page show it inline or on a new page?
If the user is logged in on a device when they reset, what happens on that device's next request? And does the reset page itself require any login?
questions.about: DELETE FROM sessions WHERE user_id=user_id (every device, incl. this one)

questions.text: What is the 'periodic delete' of old rows: what job runs it, how often, and which rows does it remove, given rows are needed for the 1-hour count?
questions.about: Purge old rows with a periodic delete

answers.text: They now see the expired page. I changed the submit flow to check the token first (plain SELECT), so a dead link never shows a password complaint; the brief also asks for a second token check at submit. The atomic UPDATE still guards the race.
Yes, RAW goes in a hidden form field and the POST /reset body carries it. The POST URL has no token, so it does not end up in URLs or logs. Stated in the file.

Yes. The count includes used and superseded rows, because the brief limits reset emails sent per rolling hour, not live links. A user who made 3 requests and then reset still cannot request another until the oldest is over an hour old. Added a line under Data.

The old link is already dead and the new one never goes out, so the user has no working link and must request again. That request counts toward 3/hour; if they are at the limit they wait until an earlier request is over an hour old. I accepted this rather than add a retry or compensation mechanism. Failure table row expanded.
The API returns the same 200 status and body in every case. Whether the client shows it inline or on a new page is a UI choice the brief does not specify, so I only noted that it is a UI choice.

Per the brief, the API checks sessions on every request, so with the row deleted that device is no longer logged in and must log in again. I do not know the exact response (likely 401). The reset pages need no login, since the token is the credential. Both stated in the file.

I do not know which scheduler exists in the system. I decided the delete removes rows with issued_at older than 1 day, since only the last hour is needed for the count. The scheduler is added to the open questions.

teachbacks.text:
1. Trigger: a user who forgot their password enters their email in the web client. The client sends POST /forgot-password {email} to the API server.

2. The API server trims and lowercases the email and looks up the user in Postgres (the users table). If there is no such user, nothing is written and nothing is queued. The server skips to step 9 and returns the generic message.

3. If the user exists, the server opens a transaction (BEGIN) and runs SELECT user FOR UPDATE. The row lock on the user serialises concurrent requests for the same user. This stops parallel requests from getting past the limit or leaving two live links.

4. Inside the lock the server counts rows in password_reset_tokens for that user_id with issued_at in the last hour. The count includes used and superseded rows, because the limit is on reset emails sent per hour. If the count is 3 or more, the server ROLLBACKs. No row is written, no job is queued and the old link is left untouched. Then it goes to step 9.

5. If the count is under 3, the server generates a raw token of 32 random bytes. It runs UPDATE password_reset_tokens SET dead_at=now() for that user's rows where dead_at IS NULL, which kills any earlier link. It then INSERTs a new row with token_hash = sha256(raw), user_id, issued_at = now and expires_at = now + 30 minutes. Only the hash is stored. Then it COMMITs.

6. After the commit, the server enqueues a job in the email queue with {to: the user's email, link containing the raw token}. The link is <APP_BASE_URL>/reset?token=RAW. The raw token exists only in the link and briefly in the queued job. The existing worker sends it through the mail provider, with 3 retries and then a drop. If the enqueue fails, the server logs it and still returns the generic message. The old link is already dead and the new one is never sent, so the user must request again. That request counts toward the 3 per hour. If the limit is already reached, they wait until an earlier request is over an hour old. If the worker fails 3 times it drops the job silently. The user gets no signal and has to re-request, which also counts toward the limit.

7. Step 9 (the response, placed here for clarity): in every case the API returns the same status and body: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." This is why unknown addresses, rate-limited addresses and successes look the same. How the client shows it is a UI choice.

8. The user opens the emailed link, which is GET /reset?token=RAW. No login is needed, because the token is the credential. The API computes h = sha256(RAW) and SELECTs a row where token_hash=h AND dead_at IS NULL AND expires_at>now(). If a row is found, it renders the "choose a new password" form with RAW in a hidden field. If not, it renders "this link has expired, request a new one". Unknown, expired, used and superseded links all look the same. The reset page is sent with Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, and the query string is not logged.

9. The user submits the form, which is POST /reset {token: RAW, password}. The token is in the body, not the URL. The server does four things in order.
   a. It repeats the plain SELECT liveness check. If the token is not live, it shows the expired page, even if the password is weak.
   b. It validates the password: length of at least 12 and not on the breached list. On failure it re-shows the form with the reason. Nothing is written and the link stays live, so the user can retry until it expires. If the breached-list lookup is unavailable, the password is treated as rejected ("try again") and is never accepted unchecked.
   c. It opens a transaction (BEGIN). It runs UPDATE password_reset_tokens SET dead_at=now() WHERE token_hash=sha256(RAW) AND dead_at IS NULL AND expires_at>now() RETURNING user_id. This burns the link and re-checks it atomically. If 0 rows come back (for example, two submits raced and the other one won), the server ROLLBACKs and shows the expired page. If 1 row comes back, it sets users.password_hash = hash(password) for that user_id. It also deletes all of that user's rows in sessions, which logs out every device including this one. Then it COMMITs. The API checks sessions on every request, so a device whose row is gone is logged out.
   d. If there is a DB error inside the transaction, everything rolls back: password, link and sessions are all unchanged. The user sees a plain "something went wrong, please try again" page and the link is still live. The server does not keep the typed password, so the user goes back and submits again.

10. After the commit, the server enqueues a "your password was changed" email to the account address. If that enqueue fails, or the server dies after the commit, the reset still stands. The user is still redirected to /login, or sees nothing if the server died, and gets no notice email.

11. The server sends a 302 redirect to /login. No session is created, and the user logs in manually with the new password.

12. Housekeeping: used and superseded rows are kept, because they feed the rate-limit count. A periodic delete removes rows with issued_at older than 1 day.
gaps: How the breached-password list is stored and queried (local file, table or service) is not specified. The doc says only that the flow needs a yes/no answer.
Whether users.email is unique is assumed, not guaranteed. If duplicates are possible, the document does not say which user the lookup picks or what happens.

The document does not say how the 'email queue/worker' is implemented, what technology it uses, or how a job is handed to it. It says only that jobs are enqueued and that the worker retries 3 times with backoff and then drops the job.
The document does not say how sessions are created at login or what a sessions row contains. It says only that the API checks sessions on every request.
Which scheduler runs the periodic row delete is not specified.
